 Judgment

This appeal is filed under Section 54(1) of the Karnataka Land Acquisition Act challenging the judgment and decree dated 23.08.2010 passed by the II Additional City Civil and Sessions Judge,
Bengaluru (CCH-17) in LAC No.238/2005 whereby the reference filed under Sections 30 and 31 (2)
of the Land Acquisition Act was allowed.

sentences.text: 2. For the sake of the convenience, the parties are referred to as per their ranking before the Trial Court.

3. Brief facts of the case are that one Appannappa, who is the grand father of first claimant is a permanent tenant under inamdar in respect of suit schedule property bearing Sy.No.20 measuring 6 acres 5 guntas situated at Kundalahalli Village, K. R. Puram Hobli, Bengaluru East Taluk.
The said land is personal and miscellaneous inam land.

As per the provisions of the Mysore (Personal and Miscellaneous) Inams Abolition Act, 1954 ('the Act 1954' for short), the said land has been vested with the State Government by notification dated 24.02.1959.

entities.text: Mysore (Personal and Miscellaneous) Inams Abolition Act, 1954
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Out of 6 acres 5 guntas, the said Appannappa had sold 1 acre 5 guntas in favour of Nanjappa by registered sale deed dated 04.05.1956.

The said Nanjappa in turn sold the said land in favour of first claimant's father i.e.
Abbaiah Reddy by registered Sale Deed dated 20.06.1957.

On application filed by the Appannappa before the Spl. Dy.Commissioner, Bengaluru under the Inam Abolition Act seeking occupancy Rights, the Spl. Dy.Commissioner based on the said application, has granted the land and confirmed the occupancy right in respect of land bearing Sy.No.20 measuring 1 acre 5 guntas under the Act,
1954 on 30.05.1960.
The said land has been acquired under the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board by notification in the year 1999.
The Land Acquisition Officer has passed an award in respect of said land.
First claimant has filed an reference/application under Sections 30 31(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 for apportionment.
The said land has been referred to the Land Acquisition Court.
It has been registered as Land Acquisition Case No.238/2005.
After hearing the parties, the LAC Court has allowed the application.
Being aggrieved by the same, second claimant is before this Court in this appeal.
4. Learned counsel for the appellants has contended that Appannappa has cultivated the land in dispute as a tenant.
Since it is a inam land, by virtue of the Inam Abolition Act, the land is vested with the State Government by notification dated 24.02.1959.
As on the date of the execution of the sale, the said Appannappa has no right or title over the land in dispute.
Therefore, any sale deed executed by the Appannappa is void and no right can be transferred to the purchaser.

He further Sri Chikkavenkata Ramanappa vs The Special Land Acquisition Officer on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/171813330/
3 contended that Appannappa has got right and title over the property only after the land has been regranted under the Inam Abolition Act on 30.05.1960.

sentences.text: Therefore, the first claimant has no right or title over the property and he is not entitled for any compensation.
The LAC Court has erred in holding that by virtue of Section 45 of the Transfer of Properties Act, the first claimant is the owner of the property.
This finding of the trial Court is contrary to the provisions of Inam Abolition Act.
Hence, he sought for allowing the appeal.

5. Per contra, the learned counsel appearing for respondent / first claimant has contended that the Appannappa has sold the land in favour of the Nanjappa before the land is vested with the State Government by registered sale deed on 20.06.1957 and Nanjappa in turn sold the said land in favour of Abbaiah Reddy, who is the father of the first claimant.
The said land is an inam land.
In view of provisions of Inam Abolition Act, it is vested with the State Government by notification dated 24.02.1959.
On the application filed by the tenant, the occupancy right has been granted under the Inam Abolition Act by order dated 30.05.1960.
In view of regrant of land in favour of the tenant, he acquired the title over the property and it will go back to purchaser.

Since any transfer by unauthorized person, who subsequently acquires interest over the property transferred,
subsequently the title will transfer in favour of the purchaser.
In support of his contention, he has relied upon the judgment of this Court in W.P.No.35109/2011 disposed of on 04.07.2012.
Hence, he sought for dismissal of the appeal.
6. Heard the learned counsel for the parties.
Perused the judgment and award.
7. It is not in dispute that Appannappa was a tenant in the land bearing Sy.No.20 measuring 6 acres 5 guntas situated at Kundalahalli Village, K. R. Puram Hobli, Bengaluru East Taluk.
It is also not in dispute that it is an inam land.
The said Appannappa, out of 6 acres 5 guntas has sold 1 acre 5 guntas in favour of one Nanjappa by registered sale deed dated 04.05.1956.
Nanjappa in turn sold the said property in favour of Abbaiah Reddy, who is the father of first claimant and respondent Nos.2 to 5 herein by registered sale deed dated 20.06.1957.
In view of provisions of Inam Abolition Act, the said land is vested with the State Government by notification 24.02.1959.
On the application filed by the Appannappa, the occupancy right has been granted in his favour under Inam Abolition Act on 30.05.1960.
The principle "Feeding the estoppel by grant" would be applicable in the facts and circumstances of the case by virtue of Section 43 of the Transfer of Properties Act.
As a result, the rights deemed to have been passed on the purchaser.

This issue has been considered by this Court in W.P.No.35109/2011 as follows:
"2) 1975 (1) KLJ Short Note Item No.175:

In the said case the purchaser of Inam land made an application for regrant of the said land and it was held by this court that if the vendor of the tenant is competent to make an application for regrant, the purchaser of inam land from a tenant would also be entitle to make an application.

In the instant case the purchaser Sri.Vajramuniyappa admittedly has not made any application for regrant of the land but on the other hand the Original Grantee himself made an application and as such to what extent the principles enunciated in the said judgment would be applicable to Sri Chikkavenkata Ramanappa vs The Special Land Acquisition Officer on 17 January, 2023

facts on hand requires to be considered in the present case.
At this juncture, it would be appropriate to note the provision of Section 43 of Transfer of Property Act.

Same reads as under:
"43. Transfer by unauthorized person who subsequently acquires interest in property transferred-

Where a person 1[fraudulently or] erroneously represents that he is authorized to transfer certain immovable property, and professes to transfer such property for consideration, such transfer shall, at the option of the transferee, operate on any interest which the transferor may acquire - 10 -  in such property at any time during  which the contract of transfer subsists.
Nothing in this section shall impair the right of transferees in good faith for consideration without notice of the existence of the said option".

A reading of the said provision would clearly go to show that "Feeding the estoppel by grant"
principle, comes into play viz., on the date of conveying the property if the vendor did not possess title and acquires it subsequent to conveying the property such title acquired subsequently would enure to the benefit of subsequent purchaser.

In the instant case, petitioner's husband had purchased the land in the year 1950 and after vesting of the land in the State as per 1955 Act he had no doubt lost all right, title and interest over the said land and during this interregnum period he has conveyed the property in favour of the Sri.Vajramuniyappa under a registered sale deed dated08.05.1959.
Petitioner's husband had conveyed the property and having lost his right, title and interest he made an application for regrant of the said land.
The authorities after considering his request granted the said land by order dated 11.10.1963, Annexure- - 11 - C.
In effect the title which he had lost or had got extinguished stood revived by virtue of order of regrant.
In that view of the matter title which was lost by the original title holder vested to him and it would enure to the subsequent purchaser.
As such Deputy Commissioner was fully justified in holding that the order of second respondent as one being erroneous since aforesaid fact had not been taken into consideration.
As observed here in above the judgment in Sreenivasamurthy's case though not applicable in its entirety to the facts on hand it would partially be applicable.

This, I say so, because in the said case subsequent purchaser of the inam land made an application for regrant and said application was entertained and considered by the authority and order of regrant came to be made.

In the instant case instead of the Sri Chikkavenkata Ramanappa vs The Special Land Acquisition Officer on 17 January, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/171813330/
5 subsequent purchaser making an application the original grantee himself made an application and as such an order came to be passed in his favour which automatically would enure to the benefit of subsequent purchaser and as such sale deed executed would not get extinguished by operation of law as contended.

sentences.text: As rightly observed in the Stumpp Schedule & Somappa Pvt. Ltd.'s case referred to supra by Division Bench of this Court - 12 - that an order passed granting occupancy rights reaches finality would be a judgment in rem and in persona.
As such the principles of 'feeding the estoppel by grant' is squarely applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case."
In view of grant of land, the title which had lost or got extinguished, should have stood revived.
In that view of the matter, the title which was lost by the original title holder vested to him, would enure to the benefit of subsequent purchaser.
In view of the above, the Land Acquisition Court is justified in allowing the application filed under Sections 30 and 30(2) of the Act.
There is no error in the judgment passed by the LAC Court.
Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.
